top_choice_rationale: P002 (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) recognises one bounded, mature discovery: estimating demand for differentiated products with endogenous prices and realistic substitution (Berry 1994; BLP 1995). Credit traces to specific papers and three people. The method has about thirty years of use in merger review, regulation, auctions, trade and health, and merger retrospectives have checked it against outcomes. The costs are real: Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin are omitted, and markups and counterfactuals depend on functional-form and equilibrium assumptions. A citation limited to demand estimation makes those omissions a deliberate choice. I rank P001 (Kiyotaki-Moore) a close second. It has the cleanest attribution and a foundational mechanism that organised a research programme and was tested in 2007-09. Its direct identification is more mixed, and it sits near the 2022 prize. I rank P003 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) third because of the bundling of technology and trade strands, the contested size of local effects, and overlap with recent labour prizes. All three are viable and clearly preferable to no award (P000). The ordering rests on judgement about weighting and on background knowledge, not verified citation data.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. No co-author or collaborator in the profile is credited on P001, P002 or P003. SSE affiliation with Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg is collegial only. My field of market and mechanism design is adjacent to auctions but distant from structural industrial organisation.
